passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Withheld Damage Deposit

emails.subject: Return of damage deposit — 3B, 220 Anstey Street
emails.body:
Dear Harbourview Properties,

I vacated 3B at 220 Anstey Street on August 29 after four years as a tenant. My damage deposit of $1,250 has not been returned, and the statement I received on September 9 lists three deductions totalling $940. I dispute two of them.

The first is $520 for "carpet replacement, living room". The carpet was already worn when I moved in — I noted it on the move-in inspection form, which was countersigned by your then-manager, and I have kept my copy. Normal wear over four years is not, as I understand it, a chargeable damage.

The second is $260 for "repainting". The walls were not damaged. I hung four pictures and filled the holes before leaving, which the outgoing inspection notes as satisfactory.

The third deduction, $160 for professional cleaning of the oven, I accept. I ran out of time and that is fair.

I would like the $780 returned. I have attached the move-in form and photographs taken on the day I left. If we cannot resolve this directly I will apply to the tenancy board, though I would much rather not.

Sincerely,
Lucia Moreau

emails.subject: RE: Return of damage deposit — 3B, 220 Anstey Street
emails.body:
Dear Ms Moreau,

Thank you for setting this out with the documentation attached — it has let me review the file properly rather than trade assertions with you.

On the carpet: you are right, and I apologise. Your move-in form does record the carpet as worn, and our own maintenance log shows it was last replaced eleven years ago. Provincial guidance treats carpet as having a ten-year life, so it had no remaining value to depreciate. The $520 is withdrawn in full.

On the repainting: the outgoing inspection does record the walls as satisfactory, and the charge appears to have been applied from a standard turnover checklist rather than from any observed damage. That is not a proper basis for a deduction, and it is also withdrawn.

On the oven cleaning, thank you for accepting it; the $160 stands.

Your refund is therefore $1,090, and I have requested it for the next payment run, which is September 24. Refunds are issued to the account the last rent payment came from unless you tell me otherwise.

I would add one thing you may find useful. The province requires a deposit to be returned or accounted for within fifteen days of the tenancy ending; ours went out on day eleven, so we were within it, but only just. If you are renting again and a landlord passes that deadline without a written statement, that alone is grounds to apply to the board.

Regards,
Priya Chandra
Property Manager

passages.title: What a Damage Deposit Can and Cannot Cover
passages.content:
Few aspects of renting generate more disputes than the damage deposit, and most of those disputes turn on a single distinction that is rarely explained to tenants: the difference between damage and wear.

Damage is harm beyond what ordinary use would produce. A cigarette burn in a countertop, a cracked window, a door pulled off its runner. Wear is the deterioration that occurs simply because a person lived there. Carpet flattened along a hallway, paint dulled by four winters of sunlight, a tap washer that has stiffened. A landlord may charge for the first and may not charge for the second, and the practical difficulty is that both appear as an item on an inspection form.

Depreciation resolves more of these arguments than any other principle. Fixtures have an expected life, published as guidance in most provinces — commonly ten years for carpet, four for interior paint, fifteen for kitchen cabinetry. A landlord replacing a nine-year-old carpet ruined in the tenth year may charge only the remaining tenth of its value, not the price of a new carpet. Beyond the published life, the item has no value left to claim, however worn it is. Tenants who ask what the item's age is, rather than arguing about its condition, tend to resolve deposit disputes considerably faster.

Documentation decides the rest. The move-in inspection is the single most valuable document a tenant will ever sign, and the most commonly rushed. A form recording "carpet worn, hallway" costs thirty seconds at the start of a tenancy and can be worth several hundred dollars at the end. Photographs with a visible date are the next best thing.

Timing is regulated. Most provinces require a landlord to return the deposit, or provide a written statement accounting for deductions, within a fixed period after the tenancy ends — commonly fifteen days. Missing that deadline is not a technicality; in several jurisdictions it entitles the tenant to the full deposit regardless of the condition of the unit.

The dispute process is deliberately accessible. Tenancy boards are designed to be used without a lawyer, filing fees are low or waived, and the burden of proving a deduction rests with the landlord, not with the tenant. That last point is the one most tenants do not know, and it changes what a well-documented objection is worth.

viewpoints.name: Councillor Beatrice Amoah
viewpoints.text: The housing figures in my ward are not ambiguous. Nine hundred units are listed as short-term rentals in a city with a one per cent vacancy rate. Those are not spare rooms; the large majority are entire homes operated commercially. I have no objection to somebody letting their flat while they are away. I object to residential buildings being converted into unlicensed hotels while families on our waiting list cannot find anywhere at all. Restrict entire-home listings, leave home-sharing alone.

viewpoints.name: Tomas Lindqvist, homeowner
viewpoints.text: Letting the basement suite is what makes my mortgage survivable, and I suspect the councillor knows more people like me than she implies. The rules being proposed do not distinguish carefully. A blanket cap treats me and a company operating forty units identically, and the compliance paperwork lands hardest on the person doing it once a month. Regulate the commercial operators — I would support that tomorrow — but write the rule so it can tell us apart.

viewpoints.name: Dr Naomi Chen, urban economist
viewpoints.text: The research is more qualified than either camp usually admits. Short-term rentals do raise long-term rents, and the effect is real and measurable, but it is concentrated in a small number of central neighbourhoods and is modest city-wide. Restrictions work where enforcement exists and are ignored where it does not, which means the policy question is really a budget question. A city that passes a restriction without funding inspectors has passed a press release.

viewpoints.name: Grant Whitmore, tourism association
viewpoints.text: Everyone discusses the housing side and nobody counts what visitors spend. Short-term rentals bring people into neighbourhoods that have no hotels, and those visitors eat in local restaurants rather than hotel dining rooms. I accept there is a housing problem and I am not pretending otherwise. What I resist is a debate conducted as though restriction were costless. If the city removes those beds it should say plainly which neighbourhoods lose that trade, and be willing to defend it.
